body:
_Researched and drafted with assistance from ChatGPT, using original Blackstone and Mitsubishi Corporation announcements, Shell plc’s SEC filings, Canadian government project disclosures, LNG Canada corporate records and contemporaneous Reuters reporting._

On 2 November 2026, Blackstone announced an agreement involving one of the most important investments in Shell’s international gas portfolio.

Funds managed by Blackstone Credit & Insurance, together with four major Canadian institutional investors, had agreed to invest $3.1 billion in a Mitsubishi Corporation subsidiary.

The subsidiary holds Mitsubishi’s interest in the LNG Canada liquefaction business.

The investors will acquire a 49.9% non-controlling interest in that holding company.

Mitsubishi will retain the remaining controlling interest.

The project at the centre of the transaction is LNG Canada, the liquefied natural gas export terminal at Kitimat, British Columbia.

Shell is the project’s largest shareholder, with a 40% interest.

LNG Canada began exporting LNG in 2025.

On 29 September 2026, Shell and its partners announced a final investment decision to expand the facility.

The expansion will double its production capacity from 14 million tonnes annually to 28 million tonnes.

The new financial agreement therefore arrives at a critical moment.

A project that has only recently entered commercial operation is preparing for another enormous construction programme.

Its shareholders face substantial additional capital requirements.

And financial institutions are being offered opportunities to participate in the project’s long-term economics.

But there is an important distinction.

The actual transaction is more specialised.

Understanding that structure is essential to assessing what has happened.

Primary sources: Blackstone — Original Investment Announcement, 2 November 2026 and Mitsubishi Corporation — Original Corporate Disclosure, 2 November 2026. Mitsubishi Corporation

Before examining the Blackstone transaction, the existing ownership structure needs to be established.

Shell therefore remains the largest participant.

Its 40% interest was not included in the transaction announced on 2 November.

Mitsubishi’s 15% interest is the relevant investment.

But Mitsubishi is not disposing of that entire interest.

Instead, it is introducing financial investors into the holding company through which it participates in the liquefaction business.

The distinction may appear technical.

It has important consequences for ownership, control, commercial rights and future LNG deliveries.

Mitsubishi’s original corporate announcement provides the clearest explanation.

The company identifies a subsidiary that holds its 15% interest in LNG Canada’s liquefaction infrastructure.

It describes the entity as its infrastructure holding company.

Mitsubishi has agreed to sell a 49.9% interest in that company to funds managed by Blackstone Credit & Insurance.

Mitsubishi will retain control of the holding company.

The transaction is therefore a minority investment at the holding-company level.

It is not a direct transfer of 49.9% of LNG Canada itself.

The distinction is particularly important because percentages can become misleading when corporate ownership contains several layers.

Mitsubishi’s holding company possesses a 15% interest in the LNG Canada liquefaction business.

The Blackstone-led investors are acquiring 49.9% of that holding company.

Multiplying the two percentages produces an approximate indirect economic exposure equivalent to 7.485% of the underlying liquefaction business, before considering the detailed rights, obligations and financial structure.

But that calculation does not establish that the investors have acquired a directly registered 7.485% ownership interest in the LNG Canada project company.

Nor does it establish that they possess corresponding voting rights at the project level.

Those matters depend upon the governing corporate documents.

The publicly available announcements do not disclose every contractual provision governing the new investors.

The authenticated conclusion is narrower.

That distinction is central to the entire transaction.

There is a second important distinction.

Blackstone’s announcement describes a $3.1 billion investment.

Mitsubishi’s announcement describes the sale of 49.9% of its holding company for approximately $1.6 billion.

But they are not identical descriptions of the financial arrangement.

Mitsubishi states that the transaction consideration is approximately $1.6 billion, equivalent to roughly ¥250 billion.

Blackstone announces a broader $3.1 billion investment commitment.

Contemporaneous Reuters reporting explains that the difference is associated with financing for the Phase 2 expansion.

The reported structure therefore combines the acquisition of an existing ownership interest with additional financing support for future development.

The precise contractual allocation, timing and conditions attached to all investment commitments have not been independently established from the complete transaction agreements.

It would be incorrect to assume that Mitsubishi has simply received $3.1 billion in cash from selling its holding-company shares.

It would also be incorrect to treat the entire amount as an immediate payment into LNG Canada’s construction budget.

The two original company announcements describe different aspects of the agreement.

The transaction is commercially significant precisely because it appears to address both ownership and financing.

Mitsubishi can introduce external investment capital while maintaining control of its Canadian LNG position.

The financial investors can obtain exposure to an established LNG facility and its planned expansion.

And the additional financial resources can support the substantial capital requirements associated with Phase 2.

Contemporaneous Reuters reporting confirms the distinction between the approximately $1.6 billion share-sale consideration and the wider $3.1 billion investment arrangement.

The different financial figures create a potential valuation trap.

A commentator might take Blackstone’s $3.1 billion announcement, divide it by the 49.9% holding-company interest and then apply the resulting valuation to the entire LNG Canada project.

That would produce a striking number.

But it would also risk producing a misleading one.

The $3.1 billion represents the announced broader investment arrangement.

Mitsubishi identifies approximately $1.6 billion as the consideration associated with the holding-company share sale.

Even using the $1.6 billion figure to calculate an implied equity valuation requires caution.

A simple calculation would place the holding company’s implied equity value at approximately $3.2 billion.

But the financial arrangements may include future investment obligations, financing structures and rights that are not fully disclosed.

Furthermore, the holding company concerns Mitsubishi’s participation in the liquefaction infrastructure business.

That does not necessarily make its implied value directly comparable with the enterprise value of every asset and obligation associated with LNG Canada.

The publicly disclosed transaction also does not establish the valuation of Shell’s separate upstream gas resources, LNG marketing relationships or other Canadian businesses.

Nor does it provide an independent valuation of Shell plc.

This is an important distinction for Shell shareholders.

Private investment transactions can provide useful evidence about commercial expectations.

But their headline prices must be interpreted according to the actual assets and rights being transferred.

The investor group announced on 2 November includes funds managed by Blackstone Credit & Insurance.

It also includes four major Canadian institutional investors.

They are Canada Pension Plan Investment Board, usually known as CPP Investments; Ontario Municipal Employees Retirement System, or OMERS; Investment Management Corporation of Ontario, known as IMCO; and Public Sector Pension Investment Board, or PSP Investments.

These institutions manage substantial long-term investment portfolios.

They invest in infrastructure, private credit, equities and other assets on behalf of their respective contributors, beneficiaries or institutional clients.

Their investment mandates are not identical.

CPP Investments manages the investment assets of the Canada Pension Plan.

OMERS manages retirement assets for participating employers and employees in Ontario.

PSP Investments manages assets for several federal public-sector pension plans.

IMCO manages institutional investment portfolios, including assets for pension and other public-sector clients.

It would therefore be imprecise to describe all four organisations simply as identical pension funds.

Nevertheless, the involvement of these institutions introduces an important public-interest dimension.

The financial performance of the investment matters not only to Blackstone and Mitsubishi.

It also matters to institutions responsible for managing substantial pools of Canadian retirement and public-sector capital.

Blackstone’s announcement identifies the participants but does not disclose precisely how much each investor is committing.

The available information therefore does not establish the individual financial exposure of CPP Investments, OMERS, IMCO or PSP Investments.

Nor does it establish their respective investment returns, fees or contractual protections.

Those details remain outside the publicly disclosed transaction summary.

The commercial attraction is understandable.

LNG Canada is already operating.

Its first phase has established export infrastructure on Canada’s Pacific coast.

Its shareholders have now approved a second phase.

The project is supported by western Canada’s substantial natural-gas resources.

Its location provides relatively direct access to Asian markets.

Mitsubishi’s existing holding company has an entitlement to 2.1 million tonnes of LNG annually.

Following the expansion, that entitlement is expected to increase to 4.2 million tonnes.

Those volumes provide a substantial commercial foundation for the investment.

They do not guarantee future profits.

LNG market prices, operational performance, construction costs, financing expenses and other factors will affect investment returns.

But the project has characteristics that are often attractive to long-term infrastructure investors.

It possesses established industrial facilities.

Its expansion has received a final investment decision.

Its shareholders include major international energy companies.

And the project is expected to operate for decades.

Blackstone’s announcement describes LNG Canada as a strategically important asset with attractive long-term fundamentals.

That is the investor’s commercial assessment.

It is not an independently established guarantee of profitability.

The financial investors are accepting exposure to future economic performance in exchange for their capital.

Whether the projected returns materialise will depend upon future events.

One of the most revealing details appears in Mitsubishi’s announcement.

The company states that the transaction will not affect its LNG offtake volumes or customer relationships.

This is especially important because LNG Canada operates under an equity-lifting structure.

Each joint-venture participant is responsible for supplying its proportionate share of natural gas to the facility.

Each participant then takes its proportionate share of the resulting LNG production.

Mitsubishi currently receives approximately 2.1 million tonnes annually.

Following Phase 2, its entitlement is expected to increase to approximately 4.2 million tonnes.

Mitsubishi says its LNG is marketed to Asian customers, primarily in Japan, through its Singapore-based subsidiary Diamond Global Energy.
